unit.can_do_en: ask for a size and colour and try something on.

brief.situation_en: Maria and Petri, a shop assistant.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.gloss_en: Excuse me, I'm looking for winter shoes.

judge.reason: Only register differences (anteeks/anteeksi, mä/minä, etin/etsin, kenkii/kenkiä); same meaning: looking for winter shoes.
Okei vs selvä are register variants; same question about shoe size.
Kolkytseittemän is spoken form of kolmekymmentäseitsemän; both 37.
Nää on/nämä ovat; same statement that these are warm and waterproof.

lines.speaker: Maria
lines.text_puhe: Ne on kauniit, mut vähän kalliit.
lines.text_kirja: Ne ovat kauniit, mutta vähän kalliit.
lines.gloss_en: They're nice, but a bit expensive.

judge.reason: Ne on/ne ovat, mut/mutta; same meaning.

puhe.text: Ne on kauniit, mut vähän kalliit.

kirja.text: Ne ovat kauniit, mutta vähän kalliit.

lines.speaker: Petri
lines.gloss_en: These cheaper ones are good too.

judge.reason: Nää/nämä, on/ovat; same meaning that the cheaper ones are also good.
Voinks mä/voinko minä; same question about trying them on.

forms.why_en: Speech drops the final i: anteeksi becomes anteeks.
Speech shortens minä to mä. Books write minä.
Adds -n for 'I': etsiä becomes etsin. Speech drops the s: etin.
The partitive plural after etsiä 'look for': talvikenkä becomes talvikenkiä. Speech says talvikenkii.
Okei is the everyday spoken OK. Books write selvä, which means clear.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Speech shortens it to kolkytseittemän. Books write kolmekymmentäseitsemän.
Speech shortens nämä to nää. Books write nämä.
Books write ovat for 'they are'. Speech uses on for one thing or many.
The nominative plural adds -t: lämmin becomes lämpimät, the mm turning to mp.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
Adds -t for more than one: vedenpitävä becomes vedenpitävät.
Ne means they, for things. Speech also uses it for people.
The nominative plural adds -t: kaunis becomes kauniit, the s turning to i.
Speech shortens mutta to mut. Books write mutta.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The nominative plural adds -t: kallis becomes kalliit, the s turning to i.
The comparative of halpa is halvempi; -t for more than one: halvemmat.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The nominative plural adds -t: hyvä becomes hyvät.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 1st person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Voin, I can, with -ko to ask. Speech says -ks: voinks.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The partitive plural of ne 'they': niitä, used after kokeilla 'to try'.
From tosi, true. Totta kai means of course.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The imperative for one person is the verb without its ending: istua becomes istu.
The illative singular of tämä 'this': tähän, 'into this place, here'.
